questions.question: Consider a computer system with DMA support. questions.question:
Consider the following two statements about interrupt handling mechanisms in a CPU.

[latex]\text{S1}[/latex]: In non-vectored interrupt mechanism, it usually takes more time to start the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) when compared to that in a vectored interrupt mechanism.

[latex]\text{S2}[/latex]: In daisy-chain interrupt mechanism, the CPU polls all the input devices individually to determine the source of the interrupt.

Which one of the following options is correct with respect to [latex]\text{S1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{S2}?[/latex]
questions.explanation:
S1: In a non-vectored interrupt scheme, the CPU typically must poll each device (or run a fixed interrupt-service routine that then figures out which device raised the interrupt) to determine the interrupt source and its ISR address, which takes extra time compared to a vectored scheme where the interrupting device directly supplies (or a lookup table directly provides) the address of its specific ISR. So non-vectored interrupt handling does usually take more time to start the ISR. S1 is true.

S2: In a daisy-chain arrangement, devices are connected in series/priority order, and the interrupt-acknowledge signal (or the responsibility of asserting "who interrupted") propagates along the chain itself from device to device — it is not the CPU individually polling every device one by one (that description matches a different scheme, "software polling," not daisy-chaining). So S2 is false.

Answer: S1 is true and S2 is false.

questions.question:
Consider the following processors (ns stands for nanoseconds). Assume that the pipeline registers have zero latency.
P1: Four-stage pipeline with stage latencies 1 ns, 2 ns, 2 ns, 1 ns.
P2: Four-stage pipeline with stage latencies 1 ns, 1.5 ns, 1.5 ns, 1.5 ns.
P3: Five-stage pipeline with stage latencies 0.5 ns, 1 ns, 1 ns, 0.6 ns, 1 ns.
P4: Five-stage pipeline with stage latencies 0.5 ns, 0.5 ns, 1 ns, 1 ns, 1.1 ns.

questions.question:
An 8-way set associative cache of size 64 KB (1 KB = 1024 bytes) is used in a system with 32-bit address. The address is sub-divided into TAG, INDEX, and BLOCK OFFSET.
The number of bits in the TAG is ____.

Size of one way [latex]=\frac{64\text{ KB}}{8}=8\text{ KB}=2^{13}[/latex] bytes.

INDEX + OFFSET bits together address one way, so they total 13 bits (the block size does not matter).

TAG [latex]=32-13=19[/latex] bits

Answer: 19

questions.question:
In designing a computer's cache system, the cache block (or cache line) size is an important
Parameter. Which one of the following statements is correct in this context?

options.A: A smaller block size implies better spatial locality
options.B: A smaller block size implies a smaller cache tag and hence lower cache tag overhead
options.C: A smaller block size implies a larger cache tag and hence lower cache hit time
options.D: A smaller block size incurs a lower cache miss penalty

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Smaller blocks bring fewer neighbouring words, so spatial locality is used less.
- Smaller blocks mean more blocks [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] more tags overall, i.e. more tag overhead.
- On a miss only a small block is transferred, so miss penalty is lower [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] True.

Answer: A smaller block size incurs a lower cache miss penalty

questions.question:
Consider a processor with byte-addressable memory. Assume that all registers, including Program Counter (PC) and Program Status Word (PSW), are of size 2 bytes. A stack in the main memory is implemented from memory location [latex](0100)_{16}[/latex] and it grows upward. The stack pointer (SP) points to the top element of the stack. The current value of SP is [latex](016E)_{16}[/latex]. The CALL instruction is of two words, the first word is the op-code and the second word is the starting address of the subroutine (one word = 2 bytes). The CALL instruction is implemented as follows:

Store the current value of PC in the stack
Store the value of PSW register in the stack
Load the starting address of the subroutine in PC

The content of PC just before the fetch of a CALL instruction is [latex](5FA0)_{16}[/latex]. After execution of the CALL instruction, the value of the stack pointer is
questions.explanation:
The stack grows upward and SP points to the top element, so each push adds 2 to SP and then stores.

- Push PC: SP = 016E + 2 = 0170
- Push PSW: SP = 0170 + 2 = 0172

Answer: [latex](0172)_{16}[/latex]

questions.question: Consider a typical disk that rotates at 15000 rotations per minute (RPM) and has a transfer rate of 50x[latex]10^{6}[/latex]  bytes/sec. If the average seek time of the disk is twice the average rotational delay and the controller's transfer time is 10 times the disk transfer time, the average time (in milliseconds) to read or write a 512-byte sector of the disk is ______.
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- One rotation = 60 / 15000 s = 4 ms [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] average rotational delay = 2 ms
- Seek = 2 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 = 4 ms
- Disk transfer = 512 / (50 [latex]\times[/latex] [latex]10^6[/latex]) = 0.01024 ms
- Controller = 10 [latex]\times[/latex] 0.01024 = 0.1024 ms

Total = 4 + 2 + 0.01024 + 0.1024 [latex]\approx[/latex] 6.11 ms

Answer: 6.11 (6.1 to 6.2)

questions.question: Consider a non-pipelined processor operating at 2.5 GHz. It takes 5 clock cycles to complete an instruction. You are going to make a 5-stage pipeline out of this processor. Overheads associated with pipelining force you to operate the pipelined processor at 2 GHz. In a given program, assume that 30% are memory instructions, 60% are ALU instructions and the rest are branch instructions. 5% of the memory instructions cause stalls of 50 clock cycles each due to cache misses and 50% of the branch instructions cause stalls of 2 cycles each. Assume that there are no stalls associated with the execution of ALU instructions. For this program, the speedup achieved by the pipelined processor over the non-pipelined processor (round off to 2 decimal places) is________.
questions.explanation:
Non-pipelined: 5 cycles at 2.5 GHz (0.4 ns) = 2 ns per instruction.

Pipelined: CPI = 1 + stalls = [latex]1+0.3\times0.05\times50+0.1\times0.5\times2=1+0.75+0.1=1.85[/latex]. At 2 GHz (0.5 ns): 0.925 ns per instruction.

Speedup = 2 / 0.925 [latex]\approx[/latex] 2.16

Answer: 2.16

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.question:
The memory access time is 1 nanosecond for a read operation with a hit in cache, 5
nanoseconds for a read operation with a miss in cache, 2 nanoseconds for a write operation
with a hit in cache and 10 nanoseconds for a write operation with a miss in cache. Execution
of a sequence of instructions involves 100 instruction fetch operations, 60 memory operand
read operations and 40 memory operand write operations. The cache hit-ratio is 0.9. The
average memory access time (in nanoseconds) in executing the sequence of instructions is
__________.
questions.explanation:
Reads = 100 fetches + 60 operands = 160, writes = 40.

- Avg read = 0.9 [latex]\times[/latex] 1 + 0.1 [latex]\times[/latex] 5 = 1.4 ns
- Avg write = 0.9 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 + 0.1 [latex]\times[/latex] 10 = 2.8 ns

Average = [latex]\frac{160\times1.4+40\times2.8}{200}=\frac{224+112}{200}=1.68[/latex]

Answer: 1.68

questions.question: A 5-stage instruction pipeline has stage delays of 180, 250, 150, 170, and 250, respectively, in nanoseconds. The delay of an inter-stage latch is 10 nanoseconds. Assume that there are no pipeline stalls due to branches and other hazards. The time taken to process 1000 instructions in microseconds is __________ . (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
In a [latex]5[/latex]-stage pipeline, the clock cycle time must accommodate the slowest stage plus the inter-stage latch delay: [latex]\max(180,250,150,170,250)+10=250+10=260[/latex] ns per cycle.

Total time for [latex]n[/latex] instructions in a pipeline [latex]=(n+k-1)[/latex] cycles, where [latex]k=5[/latex] is the number of pipeline stages (accounting for the initial fill of the pipeline): [latex](1000+5-1)\times260=1004\times260=261{,}040[/latex] ns [latex]=261.04\ \mu[/latex]s.

Answer: 261.04

questions.question:
Consider the sequence of machine instructions given below:
MUL R5, R0, R1
DIV R6, R2, R3
ADD R7, R5, R6
SUB R8, R7, R4
In the above sequence, R0 to R8 are general purpose registers. In the instructions shown, the first register stores the result of the operation performed on the second and the third registers. This sequence of instructions is to be executed in a pipelined instruction processor with the following 4 stages: (1) Instruction Fetch and Decode (IF), (2) Operand Fetch (OF), (3) Perform Operation (PO) and (4) Write back the result (WB). The IF, OF and WB stages take 1 clock cycle each for any instruction. The PO stage takes 1 clock cycle for ADD or SUB instruction, 3 clock cycles for MUL instruction and 5 clock cycles for DIV instruction. The pipelined processor uses operand forwarding from the PO stage to the OF stage.

The number of clock cycles taken for the execution of the above sequence of instructions is ___________.
questions.explanation:
Cycle-by-cycle (PO stage can hold one instruction at a time; results forwarded from PO):

- MUL: IF 1, OF 2, PO 3-5, WB 6
- DIV: IF 2, OF 3, PO 6-10, WB 11
- ADD: IF 3, OF 4, waits for R6, PO 11, WB 12
- SUB: IF 4, OF 5, waits for R7, PO 12, WB 13

Answer: 13

questions.question:
An application executes [latex]6.4 \times 10^8[/latex] number of instructions in 6.3 seconds. There are four types of instructions, the details of which are given in the table. The duration of a clock cycle in nanoseconds is _________. (rounded off to one decimal place)

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{Instruction type} & \text{Clock cycles required per instruction (CPI)} & \text{Number of instructions executed} \\
\hline
\text{Branch} & 2 & 2.25 \times 10^8 \\
\text{Load} & 5 & 1.20 \times 10^8 \\
\text{Store} & 4 & 1.65 \times 10^8 \\
\text{Arithmetic} & 3 & 1.30 \times 10^8 \\
\hline
\end{array} [/latex]
questions.explanation:
Total clock cycles [latex]=\sum(\text{CPI}\times\text{count})[/latex]:
[latex]=2(2.25\times10^8)+5(1.20\times10^8)+4(1.65\times10^8)+3(1.30\times10^8)[/latex]
[latex]=4.5\times10^8+6.0\times10^8+6.6\times10^8+3.9\times10^8=21.0\times10^8=2.1\times10^9[/latex] cycles.

Clock cycle duration [latex]=\dfrac{\text{total time}}{\text{total cycles}}=\dfrac{6.3\text{ s}}{2.1\times10^9}=3\times10^{-9}\text{ s}=3[/latex] ns.

Answer: 3
